feed.title: Crypto & Blockchain · Diting Lab
feed.subtitle: Research papers and global crypto regulation, at a glance
feed.rights: Explanations and summaries are generated by AI from the original text. Dates, rates and amounts are checked against the source, but errors are still possible, so always rely on the original. Nothing here is legal, tax or investment advice.

entry.title: UniPCH: A Unified Framework for Cross-Chain Payments via Payment Channel Hubs
entry.summary: UniPCH: A Unified Framework for Cross-Chain Payments via Payment Channel Hubs arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents UniPCH, a two-layer framework for private cross-chain payments across heterogeneous blockchains. The lower UniPC layer defines common channel state transitions and security requirements, with realizations for UTXO and smart-contract account ledgers. The upper layer introduces selective re-signing blind conditional signatures (S-RBCS) to coordinate conditional authorization across hubs, enabling a four-phase payment protocol. The authors report security properties and a Go prototype evaluation of running time and bandwidth.

entry.title: Undisclosed Fees in Hook-Based Decentralized Exchanges
entry.summary: An Empirical Study of Undisclosed Charges in Hook-Based Decentralized Exchanges arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents a large-scale empirical study of Hook contracts on Uniswap v4 and PancakeSwap Infinity across Ethereum and BNB Smart Chain. The authors analyze 7,873 Hook deployments and 50,011 pools using bytecode analysis to identify settlement charges not itemized in standard fees. They find that 24.30% of Hooks can impose such deductions, which occur in 59.23% of relevant swaps and generate substantial revenue. The results suggest a gap between displayed fees and actual trading costs, motivating explicit disclosure.

entry.title: Tight limits on fair AMM mechanism design under weak efficiency
entry.summary: Tight Characterizations of AMM Mechanism Design under Weak Efficiency arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies miner extractable value (MEV) in automated market makers (AMMs), where block builders can profit by controlling transaction order. It proves that no deterministic, anonymous batch AMM can be both incentive compatible and weakly locally efficient under plain consensus without fair sequencing, even with censorship resilience and unlimited block space. The impossibility relies on Sybil identities, over-reporting budgets, and misreporting values. Removing any one of these strategic capabilities makes both properties achievable under censorship resilience. ★★★★★ Notable: Proves impossibility of IC and wLE for deterministic anonymous batch AMMs under plain consensus, with tight characterization of strategy restrictions.

entry.title: Sybil-proof adaptive clinching auctions and their use in blockchain market design
entry.summary: Sybil-Proofness of Generalized Adaptive Clinching and Implications for Blockchain Mechanism Design arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper examines whether the adaptive clinching auction for budget-constrained bidders stays robust when a bidder splits its budget across fake identities. The authors propose a generalized adaptive clinching framework and prove that bidders gain nothing by splitting into any number of identities, as long as their total reported budget does not exceed their enforceable true budget. They extend the mechanism to a two-sided automated market maker for decentralized finance and show, through impossibility results, that these guarantees are essentially the best possible. ★★★★ Notable: Proves Sybil-robust incentive compatibility for adaptive clinching and designs a two-sided AMM, backed by impossibility results and proofs with broad DeFi relevance.

entry.title: FIDES-Live: Checking Whether Trading AI Agents Behave Consistently
entry.summary: FIDES-Live: Evaluating Behavioral Concordance in Sequential Trading Agents arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents FIDES-Live, an extension of the FIDES framework for auditing sequences of trading agent actions, orders, execution receipts, and reports. It assesses decision validity, adherence to numerical commitments, reconciliation with execution and ledger records, and report accuracy grounded in receipts. The authors retrospectively audited ten inference routes over 7,299 cryptocurrency account-rounds and a 310-round equity pilot. The paper states that its findings do not establish long-run trading skill, faithfulness of explanations, or causal benefits of audit feedback.

entry.title: Fuji: How Demand Bursts Take Shape, What They Consist Of, and How They Spread on Robinhood Chain
entry.summary: Fuji: The Shape, Composition, and Spread of Demand Bursts on Robinhood Chain arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper measures sudden surges in demand on a blockchain marketplace, using Robinhood Chain, a layer-2 network, over its first three active months and more than 50 million Uniswap swaps. During bursts, traders touch about as many pools as in quiet periods, mostly different ones, and trade more intensively, with median peaks 2.5 times normal load. The rise and fall of demand are described by two exponential functions, and the authors compare two explanations for bursts, finding externally triggered cascades fit the data better than self-excitation.

entry.title: Weekend Crypto Volatility and Monday Risk: Whether weekend crypto price swings predict Monday variance in traditional markets.
entry.summary: Weekend Crypto Volatility and Monday Market Risk arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies whether volatility in cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, Ether and XRP, which trade through the weekend, predicts Monday variance in the S&P 500, gold and a US Treasury ETF. The authors add a common weekend crypto factor to heterogeneous autoregressive models using daily data from 2017 to 2026. Predictive content is significant after 2024 and reduces out-of-sample losses, though statistical evidence varies across markets.

entry.title: Merkle-tree-based public auditing of cloud object storage using Ethereum smart contracts
entry.summary: Merkle-Tree-Based Verifiable Public Data Auditing for Cloud Object Storage Using Smart Contracts arXiv · Oct 26, 2026 The paper proposes a public auditing system for cloud object storage in which the hash and name of each object form leaves of a Merkle tree. Only the tree's root is stored in an Ethereum smart contract, while the objects remain with the provider. An auditor downloads an object and checks it against the stored root using a short Merkle proof to mark it as intact, modified or missing. In experiments, the system detected all single and multiple modifications and deletions with no false alarms, and checking one object took about 10 ms regardless of dataset size.

entry.title: Isotaxis: Optimal Asynchronous Byzantine Consensus with Ordering Linearizability
entry.summary: Isotaxis: Optimal Asynchronous Byzantine Consensus with Ordering Linearizability IACR ePrint · Oct 26, 2026 This paper presents Isotaxis, a state machine replication protocol with ordering linearizability, designed to resist adversaries who manipulate transaction order, such as in MEV attacks. Its communication complexity is O(nℓ+λn²), which is optimal when ℓ≥λn, and it is described as the first asynchronous protocol to achieve ordering linearizability. Experiments on up to 100 EC2 instances show it outperforms Pompē at all tested scales from 4 to 100 nodes. ★★★★ Notable: First asynchronous SMR achieving ordering linearizability with optimal communication and Byzantine resilience, validated by experiments on 4 to 100 nodes.

entry.title: Beyond Wasserstein Proximity: Finding Better Transfer Sources
entry.summary: Beyond Wasserstein Proximity: Finding Better Transfer Sources arXiv · Oct 26, 2026 This paper examines how to choose pretraining data sources for transfer, arguing that the most similar data is not always the most useful. The authors test five-day volatility forecasting for ten Binance spot cryptocurrencies across six model families. Selecting farther Gaussian-Wasserstein sources improved persistence-relative skill for several models. The findings are presented as exploratory results on a fixed historical dataset.

entry.title: Performance guarantees for a permissionless lending protocol
entry.summary: Performance Guarantees for Permissionless Lending arXiv · Oct 26, 2026 This paper proposes a lending protocol that the authors say carries far fewer risks than pool-based protocols such as Aave and Compound. Lenders and borrowers make competing interest-rate offers, and loans carry a fixed rate for their full term. The authors model collateral value as a random walk and use characteristic functions and Fourier inversion to derive exact expressions for liquidation and repayment-shortfall probabilities, illustrated with Bitcoin collateral.

entry.title: Decentralized medical data sharing system using off-chain storage and view-based access control
entry.summary: Decentralized Medical Data Sharing with Off-chain Storage and View-based Access Control arXiv · Oct 25, 2026 This paper proposes VASCO, a decentralized medical data sharing system that does not rely on a central server, a specific cloud storage such as IPFS, or a secure channel. It encrypts both data and metadata end-to-end, using eight chaincodes built on view-based access control. The authors report scalability tests on a 21-peer blockchain and interoperability checks across 30 combinations of standards, formats, and protocols.

entry.title: BE-CTDE: Blockchain-based multi-agent learning with anomaly detection and token incentives
entry.summary: BE-CTDE: Blockchain-Enabled Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Anomaly Detection and Token Economics arXiv · Oct 25, 2026 This paper proposes BE-CTDE, a framework that uses blockchain as a training-management layer for multi-agent reinforcement learning. A behavioral verifier compares executed trajectories with shared-policy recommendations, and token mechanisms (slashing, burning, rewards, compensation) adjust each agent's influence on the global policy update. In multi-agent path finding experiments, it achieves higher success rates under attack, even when adversaries are a majority, with collision rates up to 35% lower than detection without economic consequences and up to 43% lower than conventional stake slashing.

entry.title: Post-quantum IoT blockchain for securing edge and physical AI agents in critical systems
entry.summary: Securing Edge & Physical AI: Post-Quantum IoT Blockchain for Mission-Critical Cyber-Physical Agents arXiv · Oct 25, 2026 This paper addresses the risk that quantum computers could break public-key authentication used in distributed cyber-physical systems and edge AI. It introduces rotational secrecy, an architectural goal that limits key exposure through authenticated transitions between cryptographic epochs, and presents PARS, a mechanism for coordinating key establishment, rotation, and reconciliation among agents. It also describes PARS-ESL, an optional permissioned ledger that records only security state such as key epochs, membership, and revocation, not high-volume operational data. The authors conclude that ledger-assisted post-quantum key-epoch management is feasible for selected edge AI and CPS security-control workloads under stated assumptions.

entry.title: More Meters or More Prices? Comparing Single and Multi-Dimensional Ethereum Fee Designs
entry.summary: More Meters or More Prices? One- vs. Multi-dimensional Fee Mechanisms on Ethereum arXiv · Oct 24, 2026 This paper examines Ethereum's shift from a one-dimensional transaction fee mechanism to a multi-dimensional one that prices execution, data, and state creation separately. The authors build a demand model calibrated from 2025 block-capacity increases and find that state creation is the most price-responsive resource. Combining this model with transaction-level metering reconstruction and block-level simulation, they report that the multi-dimensional design removes fee coupling and yields more execution throughput at similarly low congestion.

entry.title: Quantum Cadence: a post-quantum consensus protocol for multiple concurrent proposers that avoids certificates
entry.summary: Quantum Cadence: Post-Quantum Consensus with Multiple Concurrent Proposers arXiv · Oct 24, 2026 Most high-performance blockchains rely on quorum certificates built from aggregated signatures, which large-scale quantum computers could break, and no post-quantum scheme matches their size and aggregation speed. This paper presents Quantum Cadence, in which each validator counts quorums from the messages it has received, so no certificates are needed. Its fast path keeps the optimal latency of Chorus, and when that fails it falls back to Coda, a signature-free Byzantine agreement. In simulations with 200 validators, its latency is comparable to Chorus and it scales better as the number of proposers grows.

entry.title: Tritone: Pairwise Garbled Disputes for Bitcoin Groth16 Proof Checks
entry.summary: Tritone: Pairwise Garbled Disputes for Multi-Party Proof Verification on Bitcoin IACR ePrint · Oct 23, 2026 This paper presents Tritone, a protocol that lets Bitcoin enforce the outcome of verifying a Groth16 proof without changing consensus rules. It extends the two-party BABE protocol to a fixed committee of N operators, and the locked funds stay secure while at least one operator is honest. The authors formally prove security against up to N-1 corrupted operators and implement the protocol in Rust. They report transaction sizes on Bitcoin mainnet and local storage measurements. ★★★★ Notable: Generalizes two-party BABE to N operators with a new Lamport-adaptor binding gadget, verifying Groth16 on Bitcoin without consensus changes, with implementation and on-chain cost measurements.

entry.title: Beyond Copying: Lifelong Smart Contract Security Task Construction via Protocol Mutation
entry.summary: Beyond Copying: Lifelong Smart Contract Security Task Construction via Protocol Mutation arXiv · Oct 23, 2026 This paper proposes CONSTRAINTDIAL, a framework that automatically builds smart contract security tasks by mutating protocols, to test AI agents on detecting, exploiting, and patching vulnerabilities. It changes the calls or inputs needed for an attack so the original fails while exploitability and normal functionality are preserved, and new incidents are added over time. Using 203 public cases, the authors built 3,045 task inputs. Protocol mutation lowered success with supplied public answers by 10.9 percentage points on average compared with reconstruction alone.

entry.title: Tracing Money Laundering Across DeFi, Bridges and Mixers on Ethereum
entry.summary: Tracing Money Laundering Across DeFi, Bridges, and Mixers on Ethereum arXiv · Oct 23, 2026 This paper presents FPTracer, a framework for tracing illicit assets through Ethereum services such as DeFi protocols, cross-chain bridges and mixers. It recovers intra-transaction asset-flow paths using a Context-Aware Transfer Tree, classifies transactions with cross-chain intent, and analyzes post-mixer activity using upstream laundering evidence. Evaluated on 20 real-world cases, it achieves the highest recall for known laundering addresses and destinations and finds 30 previously unreported bridge uses.

entry.title: A systematic survey of optimization tools for Hydra multi-party channels
entry.summary: SoK: Optimization Tools for the Hydra Multiplayer Channel IACR ePrint · Oct 23, 2026 This paper is a systematization of knowledge (SoK) survey on blockchain Layer-2 scaling. It reviews existing two-party payment channel protocols and the tools built on them, explaining their core ideas. It then identifies use cases that call for new protocols for Hydra's multi-party channels, lists open problems, and suggests existing tools that could address them or serve as starting points.

entry.title: SILMARILS-MV: An Information-Theoretically Secure Multi-Verifier Signature Scheme for Permissioned Blockchains
entry.summary: SILMARILS-MV: Information-Theoretically Secure Multi-Verifier Signatures with Dealer-Free Key Issuance and Linear Aggregation for Permissioned Blockchains arXiv · Oct 23, 2026 The paper proposes SILMARILS-MV, a multi-verifier signature scheme that remains secure against unbounded adversaries and needs no trusted dealer for key issuance. Signatures can be linearly aggregated, and the committee can sign threshold certificates of constant size. According to the authors' analysis and HotStuff prototype, it reduces authentication traffic and cryptographic CPU cost compared with ML-DSA-44.

entry.title: DLT Terms 100: A Blockchain Glossary Based on ISO 22739:2024
entry.summary: DLT Terms 100: a learner's glossary based on ISO 22739:2024 arXiv · Oct 22, 2026 This paper proposes "DLT Terms 100," a glossary intended to improve understanding of blockchain, or distributed ledger technology (DLT). The authors note that gaps between business and technical terminology, and confusion from existing financial terms being reused, hinder comprehension. The glossary is based on ISO 22739:2024 and categorizes terms by how often they appear in representative domestic and international literature and by difficulty level.

entry.title: Temporal liquidity matching for blockchains: an EIP-1559 extension admitting transactions below the base fee
entry.summary: Temporal Liquidity Crossing for Blockchains: An EIP-1559 Extension for Admission Below the Base Fee arXiv · Oct 22, 2026 The paper proposes temporal liquidity markets (TLM), in which transactions seeking early block execution (consumers) fund transactions that accept later execution (providers). In a block-local EIP-1559 extension, providers can be admitted below the base-fee floor, and their gas is excluded from the ordinary demand controller input. The authors state an adversary model with strategic senders and builders and prove eight properties, including validator-checked rule validity, full burning of the base fee, and no subsidy.

entry.title: Cambium: Shared Commitment Roots Built by Participants
entry.summary: Cambium: Participant-Built Commitment Roots for Shared Digital Infrastructure arXiv · Oct 22, 2026 This paper presents Cambium, a permissioned peer-to-peer service in which participants jointly build each cycle's commitment root, so no single party decides which inputs it includes. Fixed-size committees certify inputs, and a recursive-doubling merge spreads root construction across all nodes. A Go prototype on AWS completed cycles in 12 to 148 ms, verified proofs in under 1.5 ms, and showed logarithmic growth.

entry.title: Who Patches the Lightning Network? Release-line analysis of Lightning gossip, 2023–2026
entry.summary: Who Patches the Lightning Network? Evidence from Release Lines in Gossip, 2023-2026 arXiv · Oct 22, 2026 The paper infers which software release line each Lightning node runs by matching the feature bits it announces in public gossip against implementation sources. Analyzing 814 daily graph snapshots from 2023 to 2026, it finds nodes upgrade on release and platform schedules rather than after security disclosures. The authors suggest that platforms packaging releases are the main lever for nodes that lag behind. ★★★★★ Notable: Infers release lines from gossip feature bits, validated on daily snapshots, showing platform packaging drives Lightning patching more than disclosures.

entry.title: Using time-series foundation models to detect financial crime
entry.summary: Leveraging Time-Series Foundation Models for Financial Crime Detection arXiv · Oct 21, 2026 This paper proposes TCEE, a framework that summarizes each account's transaction history with a frozen time-series foundation model and adds the relevant temporal context to each transaction's representation. These representations can be used for edge classification or as edge features in a graph neural network. Across six AMLWorld datasets, TCEE improves PR-AUC by 10.8% on average over the strongest baseline on five datasets and trains 6.0 times faster end-to-end.

entry.title: Secure metaverse computation offloading with smart update admission and adaptive Byzantine redundancy
entry.summary: Semantic-Aware Update Admission and Adaptive Byzantine Redundancy for Secure Computation Offloading in COIN-Enabled Metaverse Systems arXiv · Oct 21, 2026 This paper studies secure computation offloading for latency-sensitive metaverse services in computing-in-the-network (COIN) systems. It jointly decides which shared-state updates to commit to a blockchain, how much PBFT Byzantine redundancy to provision, and where to run tasks. The authors propose a hierarchical R-PBFT approach combining an identical-interest game with a feasibility-filtered double deep Q-network. Numerical results report reward gains over the strongest baseline and ablations that assess feasibility filtering and adaptive deferral.

entry.title: How Not to Be Censored: Guaranteeing Client Transaction Inclusion in Blockchain Consensus
entry.summary: How Not to Be Censored: Inclusion Safety in Client-Led Consensus arXiv · Oct 21, 2026 This paper observes that blockchain consensus is typically client-server, with clients only submitting transactions and relying on validators to include them. The authors propose a leaderless consensus protocol in which clients actively participate and define inclusion safety, a guarantee that a client's transaction enters some block produced in an epoch. The analysis covers synchrony and asynchrony, showing that client or replica connectivity can substitute for one another, though relying on replica connectivity requires a longer epoch.

entry.title: PQ-Vault: A provably quantum-safe way to hold Ethereum assets without changing Ethereum
entry.summary: PQ-Vault: Provably Quantum-Safe Asset Custody for Unmodified Ethereum arXiv · Oct 21, 2026 The paper warns that a quantum computer could recover the private key of any Ethereum account whose public key is already on chain. The authors prove that sidechains or bridges cannot protect such accounts without changing Ethereum's rules, so funds must move into a vault contract released only through quantum-safe primitives. They present PQ-Vault, combining this vault, a quantum-safe proof-of-stake sidechain, and an optimistic dispute protocol. ★★★★ Notable: Proves unmodified Ethereum cannot protect vulnerable accounts without quantum-safe vault release, and finds compact certificates drop to about 60 bits.

entry.title: Regime-aware multi-asset portfolio allocation using hidden Markov models and nested clustered optimization, tested on Indonesian assets.
entry.summary: Market Regime-Based Multi-Asset Portfolio Optimization Using Nested Clustered Optimization for Tactical Asset Allocation arXiv · Oct 20, 2026 The paper proposes a tactical asset allocation framework that combines Gaussian Hidden Markov Model regime detection with Nested Clustered Optimization, with regimes identified out of sample. It is tested on an Indonesian multi-asset universe including government bonds, LQ45 equities, gold, CNY/IDR exchange rates, and Bitcoin over 56 out-of-sample months from 2021 to 2025. The regime-aware version limits maximum drawdown to 4.44%, but the regime-agnostic NCO shows a lower drawdown of 2.19% and higher cumulative return. The authors find that a rolling 24-month HMM switches regimes in 55 of 56 months, causing regime drift that erodes the expected gains.

entry.title: Why Ethereum-style SDK defaults fail on UTXO-style chains: three reusable design patterns
entry.summary: When EVM Defaults Break: Three SDK Patterns for UTXO-Family Wallets arXiv · Oct 20, 2026 This paper argues that mainstream Web3 SDKs such as ethers.js and viem assume an account-based ledger, a single secp256k1 signer, and transactions built without input selection. These assumptions break on UTXO-family chains like Nervos CKB's Cell model and when wallets use different cryptographic primitives. Using the TypeScript SDK CCC, the authors extract three recurring patterns from its release history and exported APIs: a declarative transaction composer, a unified signer abstraction, and a drop-in connector UI component. The paper presents these as transferable design lessons for SDKs serving UTXO-family ledgers and heterogeneous wallets.

entry.title: A blockchain consensus method where miners run AI inference instead of hash puzzles
entry.summary: Proof-of-Machine-Learning-Inference: Mining Knowledge, Not Hashes arXiv · Oct 20, 2026 This paper proposes Proof-of-ML-Inference (PoML), a consensus protocol in which miners perform user-requested machine-learning inference instead of computing hash puzzles. The authors formalize the computational assumptions needed for ML inference to replace hash work and argue that LLMs and diffusion models satisfy them. They analyse security by reducing it to the Bitcoin Backbone model and evaluate block-time stability in a simulated environment.

entry.title: Fortress: A Fork-Resistant Transparency Log Using Social Graph Structure
entry.summary: Fortress: Fork Resistant Transparency logs Relying on Social graph Structure arXiv · Oct 19, 2026 Transparency systems such as Key Transparency rely on external anchors like bulletin boards, blockchains, or out-of-band gossip among auditors to ensure everyone sees the same directory. This paper proposes using the social graph formed by users themselves as a replacement, formalizing a primitive called sg-FORT and constructing the Fortress protocol. In honest runs, out-of-band interactions occur only when users reset their secrets, and security is proven under standard cryptographic assumptions. The authors present this as a feasibility result under simplifying assumptions such as synchronous epochs and always-online users.

entry.title: Testing Whether AI Trading Agents Follow Their Rules or Just Get Lucky
entry.summary: The Control Layer Behind Rule-Following Agents Trading Across Market Conditions arXiv · Oct 19, 2026 This paper tests whether four AI trading agents followed their declared strategies and risk rules. The authors analysed 2,627 closed positions, mostly simulated against live prices with a 0.09% round-trip fee, and 18% using real Hyperliquid orders. The fleet finished net positive after fees with high rule adherence, and the study provides a toolkit to separate rule-following from luck. The authors stress these are trade-level results, not proof of account returns or a lasting edge.

entry.title: Peer-relative trust screening to resist label-flipping attacks in semi-decentralized federated learning
entry.summary: Peer-Relative Trust-Guided Update Screening for Robust Semi-Decentralized Federated Learning under Label-Flipping Attacks arXiv · Oct 19, 2026 This paper proposes a peer-relative trust-based update screening method to make semi-decentralized federated learning more robust against label-flipping attacks. It combines a robust validation-utility score with direction- and norm-based update quality measures. In experiments with 50 MNIST clients and 20% persistent attackers, the method reached 98.37% accuracy under moderate heterogeneity, rejecting 95.82% of malicious updates, and 95.25% accuracy under severe heterogeneity, rejecting 88.55% of malicious updates.

entry.title: On Pearl Blockchain's Proof of Useful Work: Systematization and Flexibility
entry.summary: On Pearl Blockchain's Proof of Useful Work: Systematization and Flexibility arXiv · Oct 19, 2026 This paper revisits the proof-of-useful-work (PoUW) scheme from the Pearl blockchain white paper. It offers a systematic sensitivity characterization as an alternative to the Jackpot policy, along with an efficient algorithm for verifying the sensitivity condition. Building on this, it proposes a more flexible PoUW scheme in which each miner independently chooses its noise magnitude to balance computational accuracy and mining efficiency.

entry.title: Blockchain participation games with upfront contribution commitment
entry.summary: Blockchain Participation Games with Upfront Contribution Commitment arXiv · Oct 17, 2026 This paper studies blockchain participation games where entry is costly, contributors are randomly selected, and success requires reaching a threshold. It characterizes all pure Nash equilibria under homogeneous selection and analyzes how heterogeneous selection affects who commits. The authors show a minimum-outlay reward scheme that supports full contribution as a Nash equilibrium, and note that requiring zero registration reward can raise the minimum outlay under heterogeneous selection.

entry.title: Empirical Study of TEE-Based Rollup Sequencer Designs
entry.summary: Empirical Analysis of TEE-Enabled Rollup Designs arXiv · Oct 17, 2026 This paper experimentally evaluates designs that use trusted execution environments (TEEs) to strengthen Ethereum Layer 2 rollup sequencers against censorship and manipulation. It compares separating proposer and builder logic (PBS) into independent services with a monolithic sequencer design. The experiments find that TEEs have a small impact on rollup performance, and PBS does not significantly amplify that impact. The authors also report that PBS can yield significant performance gains through more specialized, efficient builder implementations.

entry.title: A decision engine for choosing where to deploy smart contracts
entry.summary: Towards an Intelligent Decision Engine for Smart Contract Deployment arXiv · Oct 17, 2026 This paper proposes a systematic method to help choose among Ethereum layer 2 (L2) blockchains for deploying smart contracts. It uses a set of metrics and user-defined profiles that reflect different priorities among them. The authors collect major smart contract categories from a community-maintained source and six months of transactions from Arbitrum, Optimism, and Base, then compute metrics and scores per category and chain.

entry.title: ABF-Bench: A Verifiable Benchmark for Agentic Blockchain Forensics
entry.summary: ABF-Bench: A Verifiable Benchmark for Agentic Blockchain Forensics arXiv · Oct 17, 2026 This paper introduces ABF-Bench, an interactive benchmark that tests whether AI agents can trace cryptocurrency funds using public ledger records, requiring each claimed transfer to cite records the agent actually retrieved. The authors also propose the ABF agent harness, built around a working memory, and compare it with general-purpose agents and fixed-order tracers. The harness reaches 75% edge recall, versus 47% for Codex and 10% for Claude Code. The paper also notes that agents often stop early and lose recall on larger tasks.

entry.title: Classifying DeFi transaction methods using network graphlet patterns
entry.summary: Graphlet-based Decentralized Finance Transaction Method Classification arXiv · Oct 16, 2026 This paper examines whether network topology can identify the transaction methods that describe Decentralized Finance (DeFi) operations. The authors extract directed graphlet features to classify the 30 most frequent methods. They report that graphlet features complement event log counts and improve classification performance. Using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), they derive model explanations that reveal method-specific graphlet structural patterns.

entry.title: Paper on whether adaptive transaction fees stay stable across multiple blockchains
entry.summary: On the (In)stability of Adaptive Fee Mechanisms in Multi-Chain Systems arXiv · Oct 16, 2026 This paper studies whether adaptive base fee mechanisms like Ethereum's EIP-1559 remain stable when several blockchains are linked by cross-chain transfers. The authors model multi-chain fee markets as a nonlinear dynamical system with delayed feedback and identify delay-amplified over-correction as the root cause of instability. Experiments show that cross-chain coupling shrinks the safe range of update rates and that instability spreads to peer chains. The authors also propose a lightweight protocol-level mitigation that removes the over-correction.

entry.title: Market Efficiency in a Changing Asset Population: Mobility, Entry, and Survival Across Cryptocurrency History
entry.summary: Market Efficiency in a Changing Asset Population: Mobility, Entry, and Survival over Cryptocurrency's Full History arXiv · Oct 16, 2026 This paper tests symmetry restrictions implied by weak-form efficiency on the Markov chain of cryptocurrency capitalisation movements, using 8,970 listed assets across 690 weekly cross-sections from 2013 to 2026. Symmetry is rejected in every era, but asymmetry falls, and the convergence is attributed to entry-driven compositional churn rather than changes in coins' own valuations. The bottom decile shows 27.5% weekly returns on paper but none among tradable assets, with capacity of $293,000.

entry.title: QuarkShard: Splitting Cross-Shard Requests into Single-Shard Transactions
entry.summary: QuarkShard: Decomposing Cross-Shard Requests into Single-Input Transactions arXiv · Oct 16, 2026 This paper proposes QuarkShard, a sharding protocol for blockchains that splits cross-shard user requests into transactions that each need consensus within only one shard. A request decomposition algorithm is said to preserve fund or location atomicity, and the design is said to improve resistance to MEV and flooding attacks. In tests across four AWS regions, the authors report a peak throughput of 1024k requests per second with latency under 4 seconds, and up to 210.7% and 314.8% of the maximum throughput of Kronos and 2PC.

entry.title: Provable Authority: A Verifiable Protocol for Checking Organizational Authority Before Transactions
entry.summary: Provable Authority: A Protocol for Verifiable Authority Resolution and Control Across Human, Organizational, and Agentic Transactions arXiv · Oct 16, 2026 The paper proposes the ChainIT Authority Protocol, which lets a counterparty or payment rail independently verify, before execution, that the party presenting a transaction holds current organizational authority to execute it. It separates identity, a versioned authority record, sourced evidence, policy predicates, and execution credentials, binding decisions and human approvals to a canonical transaction digest. The paper also covers an extension for AI agent subjects, enforcement profiles for fiat and stablecoin rails, and stated residual risks and non-goals.

entry.title: Aerie: A proof system that aggregates post-quantum Falcon signatures into one short proof
entry.summary: Aerie: Efficient Aggregation of Falcon Signatures IACR ePrint · Oct 16, 2026 This paper presents Aerie, a proof system that aggregates Falcon-512 and Falcon-1024 signatures, the post-quantum signatures selected by NIST, into a single short proof. Aerie keeps each signature's short random salt in the aggregate, so the verifier computes hashes directly and the proof covers only algebraic and norm checks. On an Apple M4 Max laptop without GPU acceleration, it aggregates 32,768 Falcon-512 signatures in 0.65 seconds, and verification takes 54 milliseconds on one core. The authors prove knowledge soundness in the random-oracle model. ★★★★ Notable: Aggregates Falcon signatures with a lattice SNARK, keeping salts so verifiers hash directly and proving byte-format rules; benchmarks on 32,768 signatures show concrete speed.

entry.title: Agentic AI in Automated Markets: How Different Trading Behaviors Affect Market Stress and Volatility
entry.summary: Agentic AI in Automated Markets arXiv · Oct 16, 2026 This paper studies automated markets run by formulaic market makers, where three reinforcement-learning trading agents are modeled: a rational arbitrageur, a manipulator, and a retail herd-follower. A pilot on hourly cryptocurrency data (AAVE, ETC, SUI) compares how each behavior affects stress episodes, risk-adjusted performance, and volatility. The authors conclude that regulation should target specific behaviors rather than apply uniform limits on volatility or turnover.

entry.title: TCDA: Tunable Coded Distributed Arrays for Blockchain Data Availability Sampling
entry.summary: TCDA: Tunable Coded Distributed Arrays for Data Availability Sampling arXiv · Oct 16, 2026 This paper proposes TCDA, a coded network layer for data availability sampling in blockchains that remains robust against an unbounded number of Byzantine nodes. A tunable parameter sets how much of its assigned data each node keeps, trading off dissemination and storage costs against retrieval cost. At Ethereum's parameters for a 32 MiB block, the authors report that the fully replicated RDA misses the attestation deadline, while TCDA meets it from 868 to 40,000 good nodes, using 1.7 to 32 times less storage per node and 2.5 to 7.7 round-trips per sample.

entry.title: Capital Costs Protect the Network: Idle Mining Periods in Proof-of-Work Blockchains
entry.summary: Capital Costs Protect the Network: Mining Gap Dynamics in Proof-of-Work Blockchains Under a Stochastic Mempool arXiv · Oct 16, 2026 As block subsidies decline, Proof-of-Work blockchains increasingly depend on transaction fees to keep miners active. The paper models the backlog of high-fee transactions as a Lindley-type recursion and uses its stationary distribution to characterize the mining gap, the idle time miners face before enough profitable transactions accumulate. Under Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment, the expected gap grows with network hashpower and can fill an entire round as hashpower grows without bound. A free-entry condition yields a unique long-run equilibrium hashpower, and capital cost caps that equilibrium so the gap never occupies the whole round.

entry.title: Study on whether blockchain gossip protocols keep consensus messages reliable under attack
entry.summary: On the Robustness of Gossip Protocols in Modern Blockchains arXiv · Oct 15, 2026 This paper examines how well gossip protocols used in large blockchains such as Ethereum, Polkadot, Bitcoin, and Solana withstand realistic network adversaries. The authors show analytically and empirically that commonly chosen random-graph parameters may not ensure enough honest nodes receive consensus messages to form quorums. They compare protocols and report tradeoffs, including Solana's bandwidth-efficient but adaptive-attack-fragile trees, Polkadot's robust but bandwidth-heavy grid, and GossipSub's efficiency and resilience with parameter sensitivity. Bitcoin-style Erdős-Rényi graphs offer a strong robustness-efficiency tradeoff when average fanout exceeds 15 for networks up to 5000 nodes. ★★★★ Notable: Compares several blockchain gossip protocols via analysis and large-scale measurements, revealing robustness and efficiency tradeoffs under adaptive attacks.
